message: Our assembly line can only start a production run when parts from all three of our suppliers have arrived. Each supplier independently delivers on time 90% of the time. Our operations director said in the review, with total confidence: "Every supplier is 90% reliable, so we start on time 90% of the time. That's the number we'll quote to the customer." It sounds right to me; they're all at 90%, so the whole chain is at 90%. Can we quote 90% on-time starts to the customer?
response:
No, 90% is too high. If all three suppliers must deliver and they're independent, the probabilities multiply:

0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = **0.729, or about 73%**

A chain is only as reliable as all its links working together. Each supplier fails 10% of the time, and any one failure delays the start. So you'd expect roughly 27 late starts per 100 runs, not 10.

The 90% figure would only be right if the suppliers were perfectly correlated, meaning they all succeed or all fail together. That contradicts the "independent" premise.

A few caveats on the 73%:

- **It's a model, not a measurement.** If the suppliers share a cause of delay, such as the same freight carrier, port, or region, the true figure could be somewhat higher than 73% (failures overlap) but is hard to estimate without data.
- **Buffer helps.** If you order early enough that a slightly late delivery still allows an on-time start, the effective rate can be higher than 73%. The 90% figure describes supplier on-time delivery, not necessarily your start-time performance.
- **Best check:** pull your actual history of production starts and compute the real on-time rate. If it's near 73%, the model holds.

I'd quote the customer something like 73%, or a range if you have data on buffers and correlation. Quoting 90% would likely mean missing the promise about one run in four.
